title: Bees above the bus station
subtitle: A bus driver turned the roof of his town's bus station into a home for two hundred thousand bees.
text: Five years ago, the roof of Harwick's main bus station was a flat stretch of grey gravel, visited only by pigeons and the occasional engineer checking the drains. Today it is home to around two hundred thousand bees. {1} 'Most people walk underneath it every day,' says Dev Mistry, who looks after the hives, 'and have no idea it's there.'

Mistry, a bus driver by profession, became interested in bees when his daughter did a school project on them and kept him up late reading her notes aloud. He soon discovered that bee numbers in the countryside had been falling for years, partly because modern farming had removed many of the wild flowers they depend on. {2} He began to wonder whether cities, rather than being part of the problem, might be part of the answer.

Persuading the bus company was not easy. Managers worried about passengers being stung, about the weight of the hives on an old roof, and about who would pay for it all. {3} It took Mistry almost a year, several meetings and a report from a structural engineer to answer them all. The company finally agreed to a two-year trial, on condition that it would not cost a penny.

The first summer was a disaster. Two of the four original colonies died, and the honey the others produced would barely have filled a jam jar. Mistry was close to giving up, and several colleagues told him, kindly, that they had always expected it to fail. {4} The second year, with better shelter and more flowers planted nearby, was very different.

That year the hives produced almost ninety kilograms of honey. It is now sold in the station café, in jars with labels designed by children from a local primary school. {5} The money raised goes towards planting flowers in the town's parks and along its busiest roads.

Not everyone has been won over. A few passengers still hurry past the side entrance closest to the hives, and last summer one man complained that a bee had followed him onto the number 12. {6} In five years, Mistry points out, there has not been a single recorded sting. Bees, he explains, are far more interested in flowers than in people waiting for buses.

Mistry now advises other towns hoping to do the same, and three more bus stations have hives on their roofs. He still drives the number 7 four days a week. 'People ask whether I'll give it up to keep bees full-time,' he says. 'But I like knowing they're up there while I'm down here. We're both doing our rounds.'
sentences: Each of these concerns had to be dealt with separately.
They sell out within days, and there is now a waiting list.
Such fears, however, have not been supported by the facts.
Towns, by contrast, were full of gardens, parks and window boxes, flowering at different times throughout the year.
Their objections were ignored, and the hives were installed that spring.
Mistry admits that he had been far too confident, and that he had put the hives where the wind was strongest.
They live in eight hives, surrounded by wild flowers growing in long wooden boxes along the edges.
why: 'They' are the two hundred thousand bees; the hives and flower boxes are the 'it' that people walk underneath.
'By contrast' sets towns against the countryside just described, and leads him to wonder whether 'cities… might be part of the answer'.
'These concerns' are the managers' three worries; 'to answer them all' follows. E contradicts this: the objections took a year to answer, so they were not ignored.
His over-confidence explains the disaster, and the windy spot is why 'better shelter' made the second year different.
'They' are the jars just described; selling out is where 'the money raised' comes from.
'Such fears' are the passengers' worries about bees; the sting figures are 'the facts'.
